title: Samuel's Farewell and Warning
overview: As Israel's first king takes office, the aging leader Samuel clears his own name, retells the nation's history, and warns that the people and their new king must stay loyal to God.

parts.label: Samuel clears his name (vv. 1-5)
parts.note: Samuel hands over leadership and asks the crowd to name anyone he ever robbed, cheated or took a bribe from, and they admit there is no one. They had pushed him aside for a king, so he wants it on record, before God and Saul (the king marked as chosen by having oil poured on his head), that he gave them no reason to.

parts.label: A short history lesson (vv. 6-11)
parts.note: Samuel retells a repeating cycle: God freed them from Egypt, they drifted to other gods (the Baals and Ashtoreths, local gods and goddesses), enemies overran them, they cried out, and God sent rescuers like Gideon (also called Jerub-Baal) and Jephthah. One name in verse 11 differs between ancient copies, so some translations read Bedan and others Barak, and some old versions have Samson instead of Samuel.

parts.label: The king and the conditions (vv. 12-15)
parts.note: Samuel says that when the Ammonite king Nahash threatened them, they demanded a human king even though God was already their king. Having a king does not change the basic deal: if people and king follow God, all is well, and if not, they will face what their ancestors faced.

parts.label: Thunder at harvest time (vv. 16-19)
parts.note: The wheat harvest came in early summer, when rain almost never falls, so a sudden storm on Samuel's word was a startling sign. The frightened people take it as proof that asking for a king was wrong and beg Samuel to pray that they will not die.

parts.label: Do not be afraid (vv. 20-25)
parts.note: Samuel says they did wrong but tells them not to give up on God, who will not abandon the people he chose, and he promises never to stop praying for them. He ends with a sober warning that if they keep doing evil, both they and their king will be swept away.

disagreement: Readers differ on whether the chapter treats having a king as wrong in itself or only the people's reasons for wanting one, since God both rebukes the request and gives them the king.
think: When a group wants a strong leader to make them feel safe, what do they gain, and what might they give up?
